questions.q: Benzene reacts with 1-chloropropane in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃. The major product is:
questions.explain: The primary propyl cation (or its AlCl₃ complex) undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to the more stable secondary isopropyl cation before attacking the ring. n-Propylbenzene is the trap.

questions.q: Which of the following CANNOT be used to alkylate benzene under Friedel–Crafts conditions?
questions.explain: Vinyl and aryl cations are too unstable to form, so vinyl chloride and chlorobenzene do not alkylate benzene. Alkyl halides with a Lewis acid and alkenes with H⁺ both give usable carbocations.

questions.q: A large excess of benzene is used in Friedel–Crafts alkylation mainly to:
options: reduce polyalkylation, because the alkylbenzene formed is more reactive than benzene
questions.explain: An alkyl group activates the ring, so the product competes for the electrophile and can be alkylated again; excess benzene makes mono-alkylation favoured. Excess benzene does nothing to prevent rearrangement.

questions.q: Which sequence converts benzene into n-propylbenzene without rearrangement?
questions.explain: Acylation with propanoyl chloride gives propiophenone through an acylium ion that does not rearrange; Clemmensen reduction then turns C=O into CH₂. Direct alkylation with 1-chloropropane or propene gives the rearranged isopropyl product.
